Sales.meaning: The total money the company brought in from selling its products or services in the quarter, before any costs are taken out.
Sales.up: {co} is selling more than before, so more money is coming in. Healthy, as long as costs don't grow faster.
Sales.down: {co} is bringing in less money than before. This can mean fewer customers or lower prices, and it puts pressure on profit.
Sales.flat: {co}'s sales are holding steady: not growing, not shrinking.

Expenses.meaning: The money spent to run the business in the quarter: salaries, raw materials, rent, and so on.
Expenses.up: {co}'s costs are rising. That's fine if sales are rising too, but a worry if sales are flat or falling.
Expenses.down: {co} is spending less to run the business, which helps profit, unless it is cutting things that bring in future sales.

Operating Profit.meaning: What is left from sales after paying the everyday costs of running the business, before interest and tax. It shows how well the core business earns.
Operating Profit.up: {co}'s core business is earning more from its day-to-day work.
Operating Profit.down: {co}'s core business is earning less. Costs may be growing faster than sales.

Profit before tax.meaning: What the company earned after all costs and interest, but before paying tax.
Profit before tax.up: {co} is earning more before the tax bill, a good sign for the final profit.
Profit before tax.down: {co} is earning less before tax, which will shrink the final profit too.

Interest.meaning: The cost of the money the company has borrowed. Companies with a lot of loans pay a lot of interest.
Interest.up: {co} is paying more to its lenders, which reduces profit. It may be borrowing more or at higher rates.
Interest.down: {co} is paying less interest. It may have repaid some loans, which leaves more profit for shareholders.

Net Profit.meaning: The final profit after every cost, interest and tax. This is the money truly left for the owners (shareholders).
Net Profit.up: {co} is keeping more money at the end, which can go to dividends, repaying loans or growing the business.
Net Profit.down: {co} is keeping less money at the end, leaving less for dividends, repaying loans or growth.

OPM %.meaning: Operating profit margin: out of every Rs 100 of sales, how many rupees remain as operating profit. Higher means the company is better at turning sales into profit.
OPM %.up: {co} is keeping more of every Rs 100 it sells, a sign of better efficiency or stronger pricing.
OPM %.down: {co} is keeping less of every Rs 100 it sells. Costs are eating into its earnings.
OPM %.flat: {co} is keeping about the same share of each sale as before.

Tax %.meaning: The share of the company's pre-tax profit that goes to the government as tax.
Tax %.up: {co} is paying a bigger slice of its profit as tax, so less is left for shareholders. One-off items can cause this.
Tax %.down: {co} is paying a smaller slice as tax, which leaves more profit for shareholders. This can be a one-off.

EPS.meaning: Earnings per share: the company's net profit divided by its number of shares. It's the profit that belongs to one share.
EPS.up: Each {co} share is earning more profit than before, which usually supports the share's value over time.
EPS.down: Each {co} share is earning less profit than before, which can weigh on the share's value.
EPS.flat: Each {co} share is earning about the same as before.

ROE % (annualised).meaning: Return on equity: how much profit the company makes for every Rs 100 the owners have invested in it. Higher means the owners' money is working well. Shown as a yearly figure (quarter x 4).
ROE % (annualised).up: {co} is making more profit from its owners' money than before.
ROE % (annualised).down: {co} is making less profit from its owners' money than before.
ROE % (annualised).flat: {co} is using its owners' money about as well as before.

ROCE % (annualised).meaning: Return on capital employed: profit made for every Rs 100 of all the money (owners' plus borrowed) working in the business. Higher means the business uses its money well. Shown as a yearly figure (quarter x 4).
ROCE % (annualised).up: {co} is earning more from all the money it has put to work.
ROCE % (annualised).down: {co} is earning less from all the money it has put to work.
ROCE % (annualised).flat: {co} is using its money about as well as before.

Price (qtr-end).meaning: The price of one share on the last trading day of the quarter.
Price (qtr-end).up: {co}'s shares are worth more than before: investors are paying more for them. This reflects market mood, not just results.
Price (qtr-end).down: {co}'s shares are worth less than before: investors are paying less for them. This reflects market mood, not just results.
Price (qtr-end).flat: {co}'s share price is about where it was.

P/E (annualised qtr EPS).meaning: Price-to-earnings: how many rupees investors pay for every Rs 1 the company earns in a year. A high number means the share is pricey compared to its profit (or investors expect growth); a low number can mean cheap, or that investors are worried.
P/E (annualised qtr EPS).up: Investors are paying more for each rupee of {co}'s profit. The share got pricier compared to what it earns.
P/E (annualised qtr EPS).down: Investors are paying less for each rupee of {co}'s profit. The share got cheaper compared to what it earns.
P/E (annualised qtr EPS).flat: {co}'s price compared to its profit is about the same.

Market Cap.meaning: Market capitalisation: the total value of all the company's shares at today's price, or what the market thinks the whole company is worth. Bigger usually means a larger, more established company.
Market Cap.up: The market values {co} higher than before.
Market Cap.down: The market values {co} lower than before.
Market Cap.flat: The market's value of {co} is about the same.

Book Value / share.meaning: What each share would be worth on paper if the company sold everything it owns and paid off all its debts.
Book Value / share.up: {co}'s net assets per share are growing, so the company is building up value over time.
Book Value / share.down: {co}'s net assets per share are shrinking, which can come from losses, big payouts or more debt.
Book Value / share.flat: {co}'s net assets per share are steady.

Dividend Yield %.meaning: The yearly cash dividend a company pays, shown as a percentage of the share price. It's the income you get just for holding the share.
Dividend Yield %.up: Holding {co} now pays more cash each year compared to the share price (the price may also have dropped).
Dividend Yield %.down: Holding {co} now pays less cash each year compared to the share price (the price may also have risen).
Dividend Yield %.flat: {co}'s cash payout compared to its price is steady.

52W High.meaning: The highest price the share reached in the last 52 weeks (one year).
52W High.up: {co}'s best price of the year keeps getting higher, so the share has been trending upward.
52W High.down: {co}'s best price of the year is getting lower, so the older high prices are dropping out of the window.
52W High.flat: {co}'s best price of the year hasn't changed.

52W Low.meaning: The lowest price the share fell to in the last 52 weeks (one year).
52W Low.up: Even {co}'s lowest price of the year is rising, a sign of a steady climb.
52W Low.down: {co} keeps hitting lower prices, so the share has been falling.
52W Low.flat: {co}'s lowest price of the year hasn't changed.
